ALGAE: Simple water plants, from pond scum to seaweed, that produce much of the world's oxygen.
BINDWEED: A twining weed with white trumpet flowers that wraps tightly around other plants.
CABBAGE: A leafy vegetable (Brassica oleracea) bred from wild cabbage, along with kale, broccoli and sprouts.
CANOPY: The upper layer of a forest formed by the treetops.
CHESTNUT: A tree whose nuts are roasted; the sweet chestnut was spread across Europe by the Romans.
COSMOS: A daisy-like flower from Mexico; Spanish priests named it after the Greek for 'order' and 'harmony'.
CROTON: A tropical shrub with bold, multicoloured leaves, popular as a houseplant.
ELDER: A shrub (Sambucus nigra) whose flowers make cordial and whose berries make wine.
FUNGUS: A living thing such as a mushroom or mould, once grouped with plants but now its own kingdom.
GRAPEVINE: A climbing vine (Vitis vinifera) that bears grapes.
GREENS: The leaves of plants such as cabbage, spinach or kale, eaten as vegetables.
HAZEL: A shrub (Corylus avellana) whose nuts are hazelnuts; forked hazel twigs were used for water divining.
HEATHER: A low evergreen shrub (Calluna vulgaris) with purple flowers that covers moors.
HELIOTROPE: A fragrant purple flower that smells of cherry pie; its name means 'turning to the sun'.
HICKORY: A North American nut tree with tough wood used for tool handles and for smoking food.
HOPS: The cone-like flowers of the hop vine (Humulus lupulus), used to give beer its bitterness.
HYACINTH: A fragrant spring bulb flower, named after Hyacinthus, a youth in Greek myth.
KALE: A hardy leafy cabbage (Brassica oleracea) that survives frost; it tastes sweeter after a cold snap.
KELP: Giant brown seaweed of cool coasts; some kelp grows half a metre a day and forms underwater forests.
LICHEN: A partnership of a fungus and an alga, growing on rocks and trees; a sign of clean air.
LIME: A small green citrus fruit; British sailors ate limes against scurvy, earning the nickname 'limeys'.
MAGNOLIA: A tree with large, fragrant flowers, one of the oldest flowering plants, older than bees.
MARJORAM: A sweet herb (Origanum majorana) related to oregano.
MINT: A fragrant herb (genus Mentha) named after Minthe, a nymph in Greek myth turned into the plant.
MUSHROOM: The fruiting body of a fungus, often shaped like an umbrella.
OATS: A cereal grass (Avena sativa) grown for its grain; a staple of Scottish porridge.
OLIVE: An evergreen Mediterranean tree (Olea europaea); some olive trees are over 2,000 years old.
OREGANO: A herb (Origanum vulgare) whose name is Greek for 'joy of the mountains'.
PALM: A tree with a tall unbranched trunk and a crown of large leaves; coconuts and dates grow on palms.
PEACH: A downy stone fruit (Prunus persica) that first grew in China, despite its name meaning 'Persian'.
PETAL: One of the coloured, leaf-like parts of a flower that attract pollinating insects.
PLUM: A stone fruit tree (Prunus domestica); dried plums are prunes.
POTATO: A starchy tuber (Solanum tuberosum) first farmed in the Andes of Peru about 8,000 years ago.
RADISH: A crunchy, peppery root vegetable (Raphanus sativus) that can be ready to eat in under a month.
RAMBLER: A climbing rose with long, flexible stems.
REED: A tall grass of wetlands, used for thatching roofs and for the reeds of woodwind instruments.
RHUBARB: A plant with tart red stalks eaten as a fruit; its leaves are poisonous.
RICE: A cereal grass (Oryza sativa) grown in flooded paddies; it feeds more than half the world.
ROSE: A thorny shrub (genus Rosa) with fragrant flowers; rose hips are rich in vitamin C.
SAGE: A grey-leaved herb (Salvia officinalis) whose name comes from the Latin 'salvere', to be healthy.
SAGEBRUSH: A silvery, aromatic shrub that covers the deserts of the American West.
SEQUOIA: The giant sequoia of California, the most massive tree on Earth; named after a Cherokee scholar.
SORREL: A leafy herb (Rumex acetosa) with a sharp lemony taste from oxalic acid.
SOYBEAN: A legume from East Asia whose beans give tofu, soy sauce and oil.
SPROUT: A new shoot of a plant; also short for Brussels sprout.
SQUASH: A fruit of the gourd family, such as courgette or pumpkin; first grown in the Americas.
STOCK: A garden flower (Matthiola) with a strong clove-like scent, especially in the evening.
SUGARCANE: A tall grass from New Guinea whose stems are crushed for sugar.
TARRAGON: A herb with a liquorice-like flavour, essential to béarnaise sauce; its name means 'little dragon'.
WATERCRESS: A peppery leafy plant that grows in clear running water.
